overview: The Helvetic Republic was the centralized Swiss state established in 1798 under French influence and replaced in 1803. The atlas’s 1800 to 1815 interval extends into a different constitutional era. Its outline is a snapshot of changing borders, rather than a picture of today’s Switzerland or a republic that lasted until 1815.

periods.title: Revolutionary reconstruction
periods.summary: The new constitution and administration broke with the old confederation’s structure.

periods.title: Constitutional struggles
periods.summary: Centralizers and federalists disputed the republic’s direction through repeated changes of government.

periods.title: Civil war and mediation
periods.summary: Armed opposition and French intervention led to a new constitutional settlement.

items.text: Representatives adopted the first Helvetic constitution at Aarau on 12 April 1798. A printed brochure survives in the Federal Archives. The new system created national ministries and reduced cantons to parts of a central administration, a sharp change from their earlier sovereignty.

A map printed in August 1798 warned that its canton boundaries were provisional. Its maker advertised movable-type map printing that could quickly show revisions. There had been 22 cantons in April and 18 only weeks later: mapmakers had unusually fast-moving homework.

Construction workers at Mümliswil found 173 silver coins in 1987, mostly French and Bernese. The latest was a Helvetic 40-batzen coin dated 1798. This gives the earliest possible burial date; the mixture shows that a new republic did not make older money vanish overnight.

The republic tried to organize money around a franc divided into ten batzen and one hundred rappen. Its early coins used an armed Swiss figure with a liberty flag. A coin combined a practical unit for payments with a miniature statement about the new state.

Minister Philipp Albert Stapfer’s 1799 survey asked teachers what they taught, which books they used, and how long the school day lasted. It also asked whether children attended in summer or winter. A questionnaire preserves the practical questions behind an ambitious education reform.

Other questions asked about teachers’ families and children, second jobs, pay in grain or wood, and whether the school building was falling apart. Education depended on household livelihoods and buildings as well as lessons. The paperwork gets surprisingly close to ordinary family life.

Stapfer proposed lessons in French, drawing and singing alongside reading, writing and arithmetic, with improved teacher pay. His full bill failed in Parliament. Some educational councils nevertheless used the circulated plan as a guide, so rejected legislation could still influence classrooms.

Pestalozzi accepted work with children orphaned by the fighting at Stans. That institution closed in 1799 after about six months when its rooms were requisitioned. In 1800 he taught at Burgdorf and developed a boarding school, teacher training and an orphanage there.

Poor relief remained largely a local responsibility, and many communities lacked enough resources. The republic supported some needy people and charitable societies. Cantonal health commissions also struggled without effective common rules for medical practice: new offices could have much less power than their titles suggested.

sections.title: Public words and a short political life

items.text: At Beromünster’s oath ceremony on 22 August 1798, a procession, musicians and girls singing patriotic songs accompanied the constitutional oath taken by 1,525 men. The official account describes two boys representing the French and Helvetic republics exchanging an embrace. Children helped stage an adult political message.

A wooden liberty-tree board from Bauma in 1798 proclaimed “Alle haben gleiche Rechte”: “Everyone has equal rights.” The German words survive in a specific public inscription. They express the revolution’s ideal; the ceremony’s male oath-takers and the period’s conflicts remind us that its application was contested.

The constitution promised press freedom, and publications reported parliamentary debates. Critics used the same opening. In November 1798 the government introduced censorship against opposition newspapers. Readers could encounter both the promise of public debate and attempts to restrict it within the republic’s first year.

ending.text: Civil war in 1802 exposed the central government’s weakness. Napoleon’s Act of Mediation of 19 February 1803 ended the Helvetic Republic and restored a more federal structure, while retaining changes such as the status of former subject territories as cantons. Switzerland’s communities continued through this constitutional transformation.
